title: Port Horizon
event: A labor disruption closes the main container terminal for several days.
why: A port is a transfer point where cargo moves between ships and land transportation. When the main terminal closes, goods cannot move normally from vessels to rail lines, trucks, warehouses, factories, or stores.
how: Ships begin waiting offshore, containers remain in the wrong place, equipment becomes unavailable, and delivery appointments are missed. These delays then move outward through the network.
when: The risk becomes more serious during peak shipping seasons, labor disputes, severe weather, cyber incidents, or equipment failures because there is less unused capacity available.
where: The first effects appear at the port. They can then spread to inland rail terminals, distribution centers, factories, retailers, and customers waiting for imported goods.

keyTerms.definition: A specific part of a port where ships are loaded or unloaded and containers are transferred to another form of transportation.
keyTerms.example: A container ship unloads at a marine terminal before the containers are placed on trucks or trains.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A port may remain open while one important terminal is closed, so planners need to know exactly which capability was lost.

keyTerms.definition: A backup route, facility, system, or supplier that can be used when the normal one is unavailable.
keyTerms.example: Using a second port when the primary port cannot handle cargo.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A backup only helps when transportation space, equipment, and agreements are arranged before the disruption becomes severe.

keyTerms.definition: A problem that begins in one place and causes additional problems in connected parts of the system.
keyTerms.example: A port closure delays rail shipments, which then causes a factory to run out of parts.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: The largest harm may occur far away from the place where the original disruption started.

question: Which response best reduces the immediate cascading risk?
options: Wait for the port to reopen and keep all shipments unchanged
Use a secondary port and reserve rail or truck capacity before rerouting
Cancel every inbound order regardless of priority
optionRationales: Waiting keeps every shipment tied to the failed terminal. The backlog grows, and no backup capacity is secured.
This response uses redundancy and also reserves the transportation capacity needed after cargo reaches the alternate port.
Canceling everything removes both low-priority and essential cargo. It does not distinguish between what can wait and what must continue moving.
takeaway: Redundancy works only when alternate routes and transportation capacity are arranged before the main node fails.
responsePrinciple: Confirm the alternate node, reserve onward transportation, and move the highest-priority cargo first.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The closed terminal prevents the vessel from unloading safely.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Space was confirmed at a secondary terminal before the vessel changed course.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: No usable terminal capacity was secured, so the vessel remains offshore.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Missed port appointments have interrupted the truck's planned pickup sequence.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Reserved road capacity now connects the secondary terminal to inland distribution.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The truck is waiting for cargo that remains tied to the closed terminal.

cascadeSteps: The main container terminal closes and ships cannot unload normally.
Containers, cranes, chassis, rail slots, and truck appointments fall out of sequence.
Warehouses and factories receive late or incomplete deliveries.
Stores, repair operations, and essential services face shortages or higher costs.

title: Riverbend Rail Junction
event: Floodwater closes a rail corridor that carries food, fuel, and industrial materials.
why: A rail corridor is a connected route used by many trains. Rail can move large amounts of cargo efficiently, so one damaged segment may affect several industries at the same time.
how: A washed-out section blocks trains, fills nearby rail yards, and pushes freight toward roads or alternate rail lines that may not have enough space.
when: The risk increases during prolonged rain, rapid snowmelt, tropical systems, or when drainage systems, bridges, and riverbanks are already stressed.
where: The disruption begins along the flooded track and can spread to ports, farms, factories, warehouses, fuel terminals, stores, and communities that depend on the route.

keyTerms.definition: A major transportation route that connects several places and carries repeated flows of cargo or people.
keyTerms.example: A rail corridor may connect a port, an inland yard, and several distribution centers.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Closing one section can interrupt every shipment that depends on the larger route.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of cargo, traffic, work, or demand that a route or facility can handle during a period of time.
keyTerms.example: A highway that can handle 2,000 trucks per day has less capacity than a rail line carrying the same cargo in many trains.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: An alternate route may exist but still be unable to carry all of the displaced freight.

keyTerms.definition: Choosing which needs must be handled first when there are not enough resources for everything at once.
keyTerms.example: Moving medical supplies and fuel before lower-priority consumer goods.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Limited alternate capacity should protect essential services before normal efficiency.

question: What is the strongest first planning decision?
options: Prioritize critical cargo and activate pre-identified road or alternate rail routes
Move all cargo to trucks without checking road capacity
Keep dispatching trains toward the closed segment
optionRationales: This response matches limited alternate capacity to the cargo that causes the greatest harm if delayed.
Trucks may help, but moving everything without checking road, driver, trailer, and fuel capacity can create a second bottleneck.
Continuing to dispatch trains toward a confirmed closure adds congestion and makes recovery more difficult.
takeaway: Prioritization matters because alternate routes usually have less capacity than the primary corridor.
responsePrinciple: Identify essential cargo, confirm safe alternate routes, and match volume to available capacity.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The train stopped before entering the flooded rail segment.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Priority cars were assigned to a verified rail bypass with available capacity.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The train remains queued because alternate rail capacity was not confirmed.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Displaced rail freight is adding demand to the road network.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Only priority loads were shifted to a checked road route.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: Unplanned freight transfers exceeded available truck and road capacity.

cascadeSteps: Floodwater closes a high-volume rail segment.
Trains wait or divert, while nearby yards begin to fill.
Freight shifts toward roads and alternate rail lines with less capacity.
Food, fuel, industrial materials, and community deliveries arrive late.

title: Skybridge Airport
event: Wildfire smoke reduces visibility and creates unsafe working conditions near a cargo airport.
why: Air cargo is often used for urgent, high-value, medical, repair, or time-sensitive goods. Delays can matter quickly because these shipments were chosen for speed.
how: Smoke can delay flights, reduce ramp activity, affect worker health, close roads, and slow the trucks that connect the airport to hospitals and businesses.
when: The risk is highest during active wildfire periods, shifting winds, temperature inversions, and regional evacuations.
where: The disruption affects the airport and nearby roads first, then spreads to hospitals, manufacturers, repair operations, and customers waiting for urgent items.

keyTerms.definition: The ability to keep the most important work operating during and after a disruption.
keyTerms.example: Moving urgent medical cargo through another airport while the primary airport is unsafe.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Continuity does not mean keeping every normal activity running. It means protecting essential functions safely.

keyTerms.definition: A measured point that triggers a planned action when conditions become too risky or too severe.
keyTerms.example: Airport ramp work pauses when air-quality readings pass a safety threshold.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Thresholds turn vague concern into a consistent decision rule.

keyTerms.definition: Another facility that can perform some or all of the work normally handled by the primary facility.
keyTerms.example: A nearby cargo airport receiving urgent flights during a smoke closure.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: The alternate node must have runway, staffing, cargo-handling, and ground-transportation capability.

question: Which option protects continuity without ignoring worker safety?
options: Keep full operations running regardless of air quality
Pause all regional deliveries for the rest of the month
Shift urgent cargo to a safer airport and use air-quality thresholds for local work
optionRationales: Ignoring air quality places workers and operations at risk and can make the disruption worse.
A month-long regional shutdown is broader than the known hazard and would stop essential deliveries unnecessarily.
This response protects workers, preserves urgent movement, and uses measurable thresholds to decide when local work is safe.
takeaway: Continuity plans must protect workers while identifying alternate nodes for truly urgent cargo.
responsePrinciple: Use safety thresholds, shift essential cargo, and restore normal operations only when conditions are verified.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Unsafe visibility and ramp conditions prevent local cargo operations.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Urgent cargo was diverted to a safer airport using verified thresholds.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The aircraft cannot continue while local conditions remain unsafe.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Smoke and flight changes have disrupted airport truck appointments.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: The truck is collecting urgent cargo from the alternate airport.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The truck remains tied to an airport that cannot accept the shipment.

cascadeSteps: Smoke reduces visibility and creates unsafe air quality at the cargo airport.
Flights, ramp work, and nearby truck movement slow or pause.
Urgent cargo must compete for space at safer alternate airports.
Hospitals, repair teams, manufacturers, and customers wait longer for time-sensitive goods.

title: Northstar Logistics Hub
event: A cyberattack disrupts shipment scheduling, gate appointments, and inventory visibility.
why: Physical cargo movement depends on digital systems for schedules, documents, routing, inventory records, and communication. A digital failure can therefore stop physical work.
how: When data is unavailable or cannot be trusted, trucks may queue, containers may be misplaced, and partners may stop accepting automated instructions.
when: The risk can appear after phishing, weak access controls, vulnerable software, compromised vendors, or poor network separation.
where: The initial outage may be local, but connected carriers, ports, warehouses, suppliers, and customers can all lose visibility.

keyTerms.definition: A tested non-automated procedure used when the normal digital system is unavailable or untrusted.
keyTerms.example: Using verified paper gate lists and telephone confirmation while scheduling software is offline.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A fallback keeps essential work moving without reconnecting a potentially compromised system.

keyTerms.definition: Separating an affected device, account, or network area so the problem cannot spread to connected systems.
keyTerms.example: Disconnecting the compromised scheduling server from the rest of the logistics network.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Isolation limits damage while investigators determine what happened.

keyTerms.definition: Returning systems to service only after confirming that data, software, accounts, and connections can be trusted.
keyTerms.example: Restoring clean backups, changing credentials, testing records, and monitoring before normal operations resume.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Fast restoration without verification can reintroduce the attack or spread false information.

question: Which response best limits operational and cyber risk?
options: Use a tested manual fallback, isolate affected systems, and verify data before restoration
Reconnect every system immediately without checking the cause
Post administrator credentials in the team chat so work can continue
optionRationales: This response maintains essential operations while containing the incident and protecting the integrity of restored data.
Immediate reconnection can spread the attack and restore incorrect or malicious data.
Sharing administrator credentials removes accountability and gives excessive access to anyone who can view the chat.
takeaway: Resilience includes tested manual procedures, network isolation, verified restoration, and controlled access.
responsePrinciple: Contain first, operate through a tested fallback, verify trust, and restore in controlled stages.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Untrusted gate and inventory data prevent the truck from receiving a verified load.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: A tested manual fallback produced a verified dispatch instruction.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The dispatch remains unverified because affected systems were not contained.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The train is moving slowly while cargo records are checked manually.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Verified records restored normal release and routing procedures.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: Untrusted cargo records continue to slow train release.

cascadeSteps: A cyberattack makes scheduling and inventory data unavailable or untrusted.
Gate appointments, routing instructions, and cargo records become unreliable.
Trucks queue, containers are misplaced, and partners stop accepting automated directions.
Physical cargo movement slows across ports, carriers, warehouses, suppliers, and customers.

title: Cedar Distribution Center
event: A regional fuel shortage reduces available trucking capacity.
why: A warehouse stores and organizes inventory, but the inventory cannot help communities unless transportation is available to move it.
how: Fuel shortages increase costs, reduce trip frequency, and force carriers to choose which routes and customers receive limited transportation.
when: The risk rises after refinery outages, pipeline problems, severe weather, conflict, cyber incidents, or sudden demand spikes.
where: The shortage affects carriers and fuel terminals first, then spreads to warehouses, stores, hospitals, farms, and emergency-response operations.

keyTerms.definition: Combining compatible shipments so a vehicle carries more useful cargo on each trip.
keyTerms.example: Combining several small hospital deliveries into one fuller truck route.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Fewer, fuller trips use limited fuel and driver time more efficiently.

keyTerms.definition: A shipment whose delay could seriously affect health, safety, utilities, emergency response, or another critical service.
keyTerms.example: Fuel for emergency generators or medicine for a hospital.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Not every delayed product creates the same level of harm.

keyTerms.definition: Sharing accurate needs, availability, and priorities among organizations so limited resources are not wasted or duplicated.
keyTerms.example: Carriers, hospitals, fuel suppliers, and emergency managers agreeing on a priority fuel schedule.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Coordination prevents several organizations from competing blindly for the same limited supply.

question: Which action best protects essential deliveries?
options: Prioritize critical loads, combine trips, and coordinate fuel access with partners
Send every truck on its normal route even when loads are nearly empty
Stop sharing status information with partners
optionRationales: This response reduces unnecessary trips, protects essential deliveries, and coordinates access to the scarce resource.
Normal routing wastes fuel when trucks are lightly loaded and does not account for changed priorities.
Withholding status information causes duplicate requests, poor planning, and avoidable competition for fuel.
takeaway: Resource sharing and priority rules help limited transportation capacity support the most important needs first.
responsePrinciple: Define essential deliveries, consolidate compatible loads, and coordinate fuel access across partners.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The truck lacks enough allocated fuel to complete its normal route.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Consolidated priority loads are moving on a shorter fuel-supported route.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: Fuel was not prioritized, so the truck remains unavailable.

cascadeSteps: A regional fuel shortage reduces the number of truck trips that carriers can operate.
Carriers prioritize some routes and delay lightly loaded or lower-priority trips.
Warehouses accumulate inventory that cannot move to its destination.
Hospitals, stores, farms, utilities, and emergency operations receive fewer or later deliveries.

title: Tariff change raises landed cost
event: A new tariff classification has increased the expected cost of an inbound component shipment while it is already moving toward the region.
why: A tariff can change the final cost of imported goods and affect purchasing, inventory, and customer prices even when transportation is still operating.
how: The added cost moves from the importer to manufacturers or distributors, then may reach customers through higher prices or reduced availability.
when: The risk grows when there is little substitute inventory, contracts do not assign the added cost clearly, or planners react before confirming the classification.
where: The first effects appear in customs and purchasing records, followed by inventory plans, production schedules, and retail prices.

keyTerms.definition: A tax charged by a government on certain goods entering or leaving a country.
keyTerms.example: An imported machine part receives an additional charge based on its product classification.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: The charge can change whether a shipment remains affordable and how much the finished product costs.

keyTerms.definition: The total cost of a product after purchase price, transportation, insurance, duties, and fees are included.
keyTerms.example: A part that costs $100 may have a higher landed cost after freight and import charges.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Decisions based only on purchase price can hide the real cost of using an imported item.

question: What is the strongest first response to the unexpected cost change?
options: Verify the classification and total landed cost, then compare approved substitutes and inventory
Cancel every inbound shipment immediately
Pass the estimated increase to customers before confirming it
optionRationales: Verification prevents an incorrect classification from driving the response and gives planners evidence for comparing inventory, suppliers, and customer impacts.
Immediate cancellation can create a production shortage and additional fees before the organization understands the actual cost or alternatives.
Changing prices from an estimate can spread inaccurate information and damage trust before the charge is confirmed.
takeaway: Cost disruptions should be verified and compared with inventory and substitute options before transportation or pricing decisions are changed.
responsePrinciple: Confirm the rule, calculate the full cost, and compare realistic alternatives before acting.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The shipment is delayed while its tariff classification and release cost are reviewed.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: The classification and cost were verified and the approved shipment was released.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: An unverified response left the shipment without an approved release decision.

cascadeSteps: A tariff classification changes the expected cost of an inbound component.
Purchasing and customs teams pause the release while they confirm the charge.
Production and inventory plans become uncertain while the component is delayed.
The organization may face higher prices, reduced availability, or an avoidable shortage.

title: Political unrest interrupts an upstream supplier
event: A fictional overseas supplier has stopped outbound operations after political unrest restricted access to its local terminal.
why: A regional network can be affected by an event far outside its map when it depends on parts or materials from one source.
how: The supplier misses its loading window, the vessel schedule changes, and regional manufacturers receive less input inventory.
when: The risk grows when the part has one approved supplier, long qualification requirements, or little safety stock.
where: The disruption starts at the supplier but appears later at the port, production line, warehouse, and customer order.

keyTerms.definition: A business earlier in the supply chain that provides materials, parts, or services used by another organization.
keyTerms.example: A component factory supplies a part that a regional manufacturer needs for assembly.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A failure far away can stop local work when there is no qualified replacement.

keyTerms.definition: Reliance on one approved supplier for a needed item.
keyTerms.example: Only one factory is qualified to produce a specialized control component.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: The organization has fewer recovery choices when that supplier cannot operate.

question: How should the team respond to the upstream interruption?
options: Confirm current inventory, prioritize essential demand, and begin approved alternate-supplier review
Assume the supplier will reopen before regional inventory is affected
Buy from the first unverified seller offering the part
optionRationales: This response establishes how long existing inventory can last, protects essential demand, and begins a controlled alternative without ignoring quality requirements.
Waiting without measuring inventory loses time and can allow a manageable shortage to become a production stoppage.
An unverified source may introduce counterfeit, unsafe, or incompatible components and create a second disruption.
takeaway: Upstream political risk is managed through visibility, demand priorities, qualified alternatives, and realistic inventory planning.
responsePrinciple: Measure exposure first, protect essential demand, and use verified alternatives.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Cargo missed its overseas loading window after the supplier stopped outbound operations.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Available inventory and an approved alternate shipment were assigned to priority demand.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: No verified replacement cargo or demand priority was established.

cascadeSteps: Political unrest restricts access to a fictional upstream supplier and terminal.
The supplier misses its planned export loading window.
Regional manufacturers receive fewer parts than expected.
Production, customer orders, and repair activity are delayed unless inventory is prioritized.

title: Warehouse picking error affects priority orders
event: A rushed shift used an outdated location list and loaded several priority orders with the wrong replacement parts.
why: Human error can create a real supply disruption even when buildings, roads, and computer systems are available.
how: Incorrect items leave the warehouse, the destination rejects them, and limited vehicles must repeat work while the correct orders wait.
when: The risk grows during overtime, rapid volume changes, weak change control, or pressure to skip independent checks.
where: The error begins at order picking but affects the loading dock, truck route, receiving site, inventory record, and customer schedule.

keyTerms.definition: Selecting the wrong item or quantity while preparing an order in a warehouse.
keyTerms.example: A worker selects a similar-looking part from the neighboring storage location.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: The order may travel normally but still fail when it reaches the customer.

keyTerms.definition: A separate check by another person or system before a high-priority action is completed.
keyTerms.example: A second scan confirms the part number before the truck leaves.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: It catches errors before transportation time and scarce capacity are wasted.

question: What should the warehouse do first?
options: Pause affected releases, verify priority orders, correct records, and restart with a second check
Keep shipping at the same speed and correct errors only after delivery
Delete the incorrect transactions so performance reports remain clean
optionRationales: A focused pause contains the problem, identifies which orders are affected, and prevents more incorrect shipments while normal work continues elsewhere.
Continuing unchanged sends more incorrect material into the network and consumes additional vehicles and receiving labor.
Deleting records hides evidence needed to recover inventory and understand why the error occurred.
takeaway: A short, controlled pause with verification is usually less costly than allowing incorrect orders to spread through the network.
responsePrinciple: Contain the affected work, preserve records, verify priority orders, and restart with a check.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The truck is held while priority loads are checked against the correct item list.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Verified orders were reloaded and released with corrected inventory records.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: Repeated returns and corrections continue to consume the truck's route capacity.

cascadeSteps: An outdated location list causes workers to select incorrect replacement parts.
Wrong items are loaded onto a priority delivery.
The destination rejects the shipment and requests the correct order.
Vehicles, workers, and inventory are used twice while the actual need remains unmet.
